paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Guangxi, recorded as 1960. Liu Bao takes its name from the town of Liubao, and as a [dark tea](dark:definition) its leaf is piled after it is made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes darken and soften it before it is packed away to age. The year falls in the decades when the [river trade had already been cut](liu-bao:history) and production kept falling as the planned economy changed who could buy and sell tea.

Sixty-six years on, it is far past the decade after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how it was kept matters as much as how long. Liu Bao this old is mostly [old stock](liu-bao:old-stock) that sat in warehouses in Malaysia or Hong Kong after the mining trade ended. Such tea is hard to date, so the trade reads its age from the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it, and the place it was stored gives each lot its own character.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
